- When sentiment is consistently high (≥0.8) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is low (≤0.4) and prices are trending upward, model often underestimates; adjust forecast upward by 1–2% if recent price momentum is strong.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), model frequently overshoots in subsequent days; apply a “cool-down” correction: reduce forecast by 2–5% for 2–3 days post-spike.
- If sentiment is mixed (0.4–0.8) and price is near recent mean, model often fails to mean-revert; use 3–5 day moving average of past 10–15 days as baseline for correction.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to over-predict in early periods (days 1–7) when sentiment is volatile; apply a “lag correction”: subtract 0.5–1.5% from first 3–5 forecast days if sentiment is erratic.
- When sentiment is high and price is rising, model often fails to capture “sentiment-driven momentum”; add a 1–2% upward bias only if sentiment > 0.8 and price > 75% of 30-day mean.
- If sentiment is low and price is falling, model often undercorrects; add 0.5–1.5% downward bias if sentiment < 0.4 and price < 70% of 30-day mean.
